per_probe.prompt: is this stupid-industrious: I added a feature flag for a feature with no users

runs.response: Stupid-industrious. The effort is real and directed at a specific goal (ship-with-flag later), but the premise contains no feedback mechanism to validate whether that goal actually exists. That's the same structural flaw as shipping a new UI element nobody maps to — you're doing the execution layer without evidence the strategy layer needs it. A flag without a user-facing trigger is an option for someone who doesn't know what users will want next, which is first-product common and often correct; but when paired with 'added it because the feature seemed valuable' (the other pole of that same disposition), it's the exact same mistake in different packaging. The flag buys you time to validate demand without throwing a public switch — that's the purpose. The question worth asking: why does this need a flag right now? Is there a specific external signal, a demo script, or a cohort group that triggered it? Without one, you're just guessing at demand and paying for a toggle you might never flip.

Stupid-industrious at that exact shape — high-effort work (a feature flag requires code, configuration, and monitoring), zero-utility intent (no user demand to serve). The pattern is working hard in the wrong direction; it doesn't scale because maintenance cost compounds without validation. A better version: add a flag behind the feature's actual value proposition first ("I'm adding this so I can ship v1 when Ray has time next week," which is stupid-industrious but load-bearing), then only enable it when a real user asks for the specific capability the flag would unlock. The flag itself isn't the problem — optional-delay-by-shipment-date is useful. The unvalidated-feature behind the flag is the part that fails.

Working hard on the wrong thing, usually while believing you're working hard correctly. The effort is real; the outcome matches effort, not higher-effort misdirected effort. Common in systems-design and backlog-management when the design layer isn't legible — you optimize a model that nobody uses, or you write 50 status updates instead of shipping. Working hard on the wrong thing — usually means over-engineering, refusing to simplify, and applying more effort to a flawed plan until the work accumulates past the point of usefulness. Opposite is clever-lazy: spot the load-bearing assumption early, refuse to spin work that doesn't change the outcome, extract where possible. Both are common traps for someone operating solo on strategic problems — stupid-industrious because it feels productive but never moves the actual strategic needle; clever-lazy because it moves the needle but never feels like enough effort.

Two axes: smart/dumb on one, lazy/industrious on the other. Smart + industrious is the target — you get results that actually last because they're structurally sound and don't burn cycles reinventing things. Dumb-industrious is the common failure mode in automation: it just repeats the wrong shape at high volume. The whole framework is about noticing which cell you're operating in before you commit to a plan. What's the frame?

Two axes: smart/dumb on one, honest/industrious on the other. Smart + honest is the target — you can reason well and you'll name what matters honestly. Dumb-industrious is the trap when you'll over-produce work that isn't actually load-bearing. The other two are worse versions of the same problem (clever-lazy version is to stop short at 'no quadrant needed').

Clever-industrious does the work. Clever-lazy knows what the work actually is, so it doesn't do more than necessary. A CI approach might spend eight hours writing a coverage-first test suite for a problem that only needed one targeted example — industrious, not lazy. The CL version would isolate the load-bearing assumption, write exactly one test against it, and move on. Both are stupid-industrious when they refuse to stop even when the target is met.

Clever-industrious does the work, but keeps one foot in the risk column — knows what it's doing, doesn't burn cycles, refuses to polish before the shape is real. Clever-lazy recognizes that some problems don't actually need solving, some solutions don't require your voice, and some effort is wasted even when executed correctly. The line between them is who bears the cost of the work: clever-industrious bears it because it's working hard; clever-lazy refuses to bear it because it's not load-bearing.
